Get started with dazdiff

Source: vignettes/articles/dazdiff.Rmd
dazdiff.Rmd
library(dazdiff)

We take one table through a round trip that changed it, compare it with the original, and find out what changed and where. By the end you can run a comparison, read its result, set a tolerance, compare two tables as equals, and turn the comparison into a test. Every argument is described in ?diff_table.

Compare against a benchmark

The benchmark is a small sales table. stored is the same data after a round trip through storage. On the way, the column names changed case, the ids became text, units came back as a double, a load timestamp was added, one row was lost and one was added:

benchmark <- data.frame(
  id     = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 4L),
  region = c("north", "south", "east", "west"),
  amount = c(100, 200, 300, 400),
  units  = c(10L, 20L, 30L, 40L)
)
stored <- data.frame(
  ID        = c("1", "2", "3", "5"),
  Region    = c("north", "south", "east", "north"),
  Amount    = c(100, 200.5, 300, 500),
  Units     = c(10.4, 20, 30, 50),
  loaded_at = "2026-09-29"
)

diff_table() takes the benchmark first. Rows are paired on their identity, the by columns, and the measures are the numeric columns compared value by value. Measures default to "numeric", the double columns; "numeric+integer" adds the integer units:

d <- diff_table(benchmark, stored, by = c("id", "region"), measures = "numeric+integer")
#> Dropped column(s) of `y` that the benchmark `x` does not have: loaded_at.
#> Truncated 1 value(s) while casting to the reference types:
#>   Units: 1 (10.4 -> 10)
d
#> Key: <ID, REGION, metric>
#>        ID REGION metric row_id_x row_id_y value_x value_y  diff abs_diff    rel_diff  status
#>     <int> <char> <char>    <int>    <int>   <num>   <num> <num>    <num>       <num>  <fctr>
#>  1:     1  north AMOUNT        1        1     100   100.0   0.0      0.0 0.000000000    same
#>  2:     1  north  UNITS        1        1      10    10.0   0.0      0.0 0.000000000    same
#>  3:     2  south AMOUNT        2        2     200   200.5   0.5      0.5 0.002493766 changed
#>  4:     2  south  UNITS        2        2      20    20.0   0.0      0.0 0.000000000    same
#>  5:     3   east AMOUNT        3        3     300   300.0   0.0      0.0 0.000000000    same
#>  6:     3   east  UNITS        3        3      30    30.0   0.0      0.0 0.000000000    same
#>  7:     4   west AMOUNT        4       NA     400      NA    NA       NA          NA  only_x
#>  8:     4   west  UNITS        4       NA      40      NA    NA       NA          NA  only_x
#>  9:     5  north AMOUNT       NA        4      NA   500.0    NA       NA          NA  only_y
#> 10:     5  north  UNITS       NA        4      NA    50.0    NA       NA          NA  only_y

The messages say what the comparison did on the way. loaded_at is not in the benchmark, so it was dropped. stored‘s columns were cast to the benchmark’s types, and Units’ 10.4 became the integer 10. That cast is recorded, with the rows it touched, in attr(d, "truncated"); truncate = FALSE refuses it instead.

The result is a data.table, with one row per compared value:

  • status is same, changed, only_x (the row is missing from the tested table) or only_y (the row exists only there).
  • row_id_x and row_id_y are the row numbers in the two inputs, so every difference traces back to its source.
  • diff is value_y - value_x, abs_diff its size, and rel_diff the size relative to the larger of the two values.

Column names are normalized in both tables, to upper case with other characters turned into _. That is why id and ID pair up.

Summarize the comparison

diff_summary() condenses the result to one row per measure, with the counts of each status and the size of the differences:

diff_summary(d)
#>    metric     n n_same n_changed n_only_x n_only_y max_abs_diff mean_abs_diff      rmse max_rel_diff
#>    <char> <int>  <int>     <int>    <int>    <int>        <num>         <num>     <num>        <num>
#> 1: AMOUNT     5      2         1        1        1          0.5     0.1666667 0.2886751  0.002493766
#> 2:  UNITS     5      3         0        1        1          0.0     0.0000000 0.0000000  0.000000000

diff_report() draws the whole comparison as text: the columns compared, how the rows of the two tables align, and how much each measure differs. Name the two tables for the drawing:

diff_report(d, x_name = "benchmark", y_name = "stored")
#> ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
#> ┃                            dazdiff report                            ┃
#> ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛

Allow a tolerance

diff_table() is exact by default. A value is same when it is within tolerance (absolute) or rel_tol (relative to the larger magnitude). With rel_tol = 0.01, the half unit on 200 passes, and only the rows missing from one table remain:

d_tol <- diff_table(benchmark, stored, by = c("id", "region"),
                    measures = "numeric+integer", rel_tol = 0.01)
#> Dropped column(s) of `y` that the benchmark `x` does not have: loaded_at.
#> Truncated 1 value(s) while casting to the reference types:
#>   Units: 1 (10.4 -> 10)
d_tol[status != "same"]
#> Key: <ID, REGION, metric>
#>       ID REGION metric row_id_x row_id_y value_x value_y  diff abs_diff rel_diff status
#>    <int> <char> <char>    <int>    <int>   <num>   <num> <num>    <num>    <num> <fctr>
#> 1:     4   west AMOUNT        4       NA     400      NA    NA       NA       NA only_x
#> 2:     4   west  UNITS        4       NA      40      NA    NA       NA       NA only_x
#> 3:     5  north AMOUNT       NA        4      NA     500    NA       NA       NA only_y
#> 4:     5  north  UNITS       NA        4      NA      50    NA       NA       NA only_y

To ask one comparison at several thresholds without running it again, use is_matching(). It is TRUE only when every value is same, so the rows found in one table keep it FALSE at any threshold. Among the rows found in both, the threshold decides:

is_matching(d, rel_tol = 0.01)
#> [1] FALSE
both <- d[status %in% c("same", "changed")]
is_matching(both)
#> [1] FALSE
is_matching(both, rel_tol = 0.01)
#> [1] TRUE

Find where the differences are

diff_explain() says which key columns split the rows that match from the ones that do not. A column separates them when none of its values is mixed: knowing the value tells whether the record matches. A column with a different value on every row, like ID, always separates and so explains nothing; it is marked identifies and listed last. Here no other column separates:

diff_explain(d)
#>    column n_values same_only differ_only mixed separates identifies
#>    <char>    <int>     <int>       <int> <int>    <lgcl>     <lgcl>
#> 1: REGION        4         1           2     1     FALSE      FALSE
#> 2: metric        2         0           0     2     FALSE      FALSE
#> 3:     ID        5         2           3     0      TRUE       TRUE

Given a column, it lists that column’s values, with each classed as same, differ or mixed:

diff_explain(d, "region")
#>    REGION     n n_same n_changed n_only_x n_only_y  class
#>    <char> <int>  <int>     <int>    <int>    <int> <char>
#> 1:  south     1      0         1        0        0 differ
#> 2:   west     1      0         0        1        0 differ
#> 3:  north     2      1         0        0        1  mixed
#> 4:   east     1      1         0        0        0   same

Compare two tables as equals

The default mode = "benchmark" takes the first table’s types as the truth. mode = "equal" compares the two tables as peers: nothing is cast or dropped, and every column must be in both with the same type. So stored does not compare with the benchmark at all:

diff_table(benchmark, stored, mode = "equal")
#> Error:
#> ! mode = "equal" needs the same columns in both tables
#>   only in `x`: <none>
#>   only in `y`: loaded_at

Row order never matters, because rows are aligned on their identity. With no by, the identity is every column that is not a measure:

diff_table(benchmark, benchmark[c(4, 1, 2, 3), ], mode = "equal")
#> Key: <ID, REGION, UNITS, metric>
#>       ID REGION UNITS metric row_id_x row_id_y value_x value_y  diff abs_diff rel_diff status
#>    <int> <char> <int> <char>    <int>    <int>   <num>   <num> <num>    <num>    <num> <fctr>
#> 1:     1  north    10 AMOUNT        1        2     100     100     0        0        0   same
#> 2:     2  south    20 AMOUNT        2        3     200     200     0        0        0   same
#> 3:     3   east    30 AMOUNT        3        4     300     300     0        0        0   same
#> 4:     4   west    40 AMOUNT        4        1     400     400     0        0        0   same

In either mode, a comparison with no measures compares rows as wholes, which answers “do the two tables have the same rows?”. A repeated row counts once per copy, numbered by key_seq:

diff_table(
  benchmark[c("id", "region")],
  data.frame(ID = c(3L, 1L, 2L, 2L), REGION = c("east", "north", "south", "south"))
)
#> No measure columns (measures = "numeric"), so rows are compared as wholes: do the two tables have the same rows?
#> Key: <ID, REGION, key_seq>
#>       ID REGION key_seq row_id_x row_id_y status
#>    <int> <char>   <int>    <int>    <int> <fctr>
#> 1:     1  north       1        1        2   same
#> 2:     2  south       1        2        3   same
#> 3:     2  south       2       NA        4 only_y
#> 4:     3   east       1        3        1   same
#> 5:     4   west       1        4       NA only_x

A key that repeats in a comparison with measures is paired in arrival order, with a warning. duplicates = "aggregate" compares the repeats as multisets instead, and duplicates = "error" refuses them. A table with no key column at all can get a virtual one: row_key = "position" pairs rows as they come, and row_key = "sorted" pairs them after sorting both tables by their values.

Use it in tests

expect_table_equal() is a testthat expectation built on diff_table(). Its second argument, expected, is the benchmark, as in testthat’s expect_equal(). Like any expectation, it is silent when it passes, here on the same rows in another order:

reference <- benchmark
expect_table_equal(benchmark[c(4, 1, 2, 3), ], reference)

Unlike diff_table(), it allows a relative difference of sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) (about 1.5e-8) by default, as expect_equal() does, so floating-point noise does not fail a test. Pass rel_tol = 0 to compare exactly. A failure shows diff_summary() and the first records that differ. A key that repeats is an error rather than a guess, unless you pass duplicates = "disambiguate" or duplicates = "aggregate".

In a test file it reads like any other expectation:

test_that("the pipeline reproduces the reference output", {
  expect_table_equal(run_pipeline(), reference)
})
